case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms-Burton Act allows a U.S. national who acquired ownership of a certified Cuba expropriation claim after March 12, 1996, to sue entities that “traffic” in the confiscated property, or whether the Act bars such suits unless the plaintiff owned the claim as of that 1996 cutoff date.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms-Burton Act), principally 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (cause of action for a U.S. national who “owns the claim” against any person who “traffics”), and the limiting language in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(4) addressing actions based on claims to property confiscated before March 12, 1996.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that § 6082(a)(1)(A) creates a broad cause of action for any current U.S. national who owns a claim to confiscated property and that § 6082(a)(4)’s March 12, 1996 reference should not be read to categorically bar suits by later-acquiring owners of certified claims. In petitioner’s view, the Eleventh Circuit’s interpretation improperly narrows Congress’s chosen enforcement mechanism, undermines deterrence of post-1996 trafficking, and defeats Congress’s remedial purpose of providing compensation and leverage against foreign exploitation of confiscated American property. Petitioner also emphasizes that certified claims (like Havana Docks’) were intended to be actionable and that the statute’s text, structure, and purpose are better read to focus on when the confiscation occurred (pre-1996) and/or on limiting liability in a narrower way than an across-the-board bar for post-1996 claim owners.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents contend that § 6082(a)(4) imposes an explicit ownership cutoff: for property confiscated before March 12, 1996, only plaintiffs who owned the claim as of that date may sue. They argue that petitioner’s reading would nullify or severely dilute the statutory limitation, enabling trafficking suits by assignees and successors who acquired claims after Helms-Burton’s enactment and thereby expanding liability far beyond what Congress specified. Respondents also emphasize reliance and foreign-relations concerns raised by allowing an enlarged pool of potential plaintiffs and argue that petitioner’s broader interpretation conflicts with the statutory text as construed by the Eleventh Circuit.

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any U.S. national who presently “owns the claim,” which would ordinarily include later assignees; but as Justice Kagan persuasively explains, that reading would substantially drain § 6082(a)(4) of operative effect by allowing easy circumvention of Congress’s express pre–March 12, 1996 ownership cutoff for older confiscations. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Sprint v. APCC is helpful in framing the default rule that assignees can sue, but Sprint itself presupposes the absence of a statutory restriction—and here (a)(4) supplies a specific, date-certain limitation that must control the general authorization in (a)(1)(A) to avoid surplusage and respect Congress’s calibrated scheme. A minimalist, legitimacy-preserving approach is to hold only that for actions “based on” pre-1996 confiscations, (a)(4) conditions who may sue on ownership by the cutoff date, without announcing broader rules about assignment under Title III in other settings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any U.S. national who presently “owns the claim,” which would ordinarily include assignees, and Sprint confirms that baseline absent statutory limitation. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 6082(a)(4) expressly adds a date-certain ownership requirement—"acquires ownership of the claim before March 12, 1996"—for actions based on pre‑1996 confiscations, and the specific limitation must govern the general authorization to avoid rendering (a)(4) largely surplusage. Sprint therefore does not undermine the respondent’s reading because it presupposes statutory silence, whereas Congress here spoke in clear temporal terms. Under an original public meaning approach, we must enforce the cutoff Congress enacted, even if it narrows the remedial scope and forecloses post‑1996 purchasers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any U.S. national who presently “owns the claim,” which in ordinary assignment law would include later assignees. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain, that reading would largely nullify § 6082(a)(4)’s express, date-certain requirement for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations that the claim be acquired before that date, violating the specific-controls-general and anti-surplusage canons. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Sprint v. APCC does not alter the analysis because Sprint’s default rule about assignee standing yields where Congress has imposed an explicit statutory limitation on who may sue, and here Congress did so in plain temporal terms. The administrable cutoff also aligns with the statute’s calibrated exposure and foreign-relations sensitivities, so I would affirm the dismissal of this post-1996-acquired claim.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) speaks in the present tense—whoever now “owns the claim” may sue—and Sprint supports assignee standing when Congress has not said otherwise. But as Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts stress, § 6082(a)(4) is not just descriptive; it adds an explicit, date-certain ownership-as-of requirement for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, and reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post-1996 purchasers would largely nullify that limitation. Justice Jackson’s practical-consequences framing also matters to me: allowing an open-ended secondary market in older claims would expand liability in a way Congress plausibly sought to avoid in a foreign-affairs-sensitive statute, and I do not see a clear textual command to take that step. Under my pragmatic approach, I remain persuaded the best reading is to enforce the cutoff Congress wrote rather than judicially reopening this category of suits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes any U.S. national who presently “owns the claim” to sue, which naturally includes assignees. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post–March 12, 1996 acquisitions for pre-1996 confiscations largely drains § 6082(a)(4)’s date-certain ownership limitation of operative force, contrary to basic coherence and anti-surplusage principles. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Sprint v. APCC helps confirm the boundary: assignee standing is a default only when Congress has not spoken, and here Congress did speak by tying eligibility for pre-1996 confiscations to ownership acquired before the cutoff. The more workable harmonization is that (a)(4) qualifies (a)(1)(A) in this category, enforcing Congress’s calibrated temporal restriction without rewriting the remedial scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the present-tense phrasing in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—a U.S. national who “owns the claim” may sue—so later assignees should qualify. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that reading largely nullifies § 6082(a)(4)’s explicit requirement that, for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, the plaintiff must have “acquire[d] ownership of the claim before” that date; under our anti-surplusage and specific-controls-general principles (RadLAX), the specific temporal eligibility limit must do real work. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Sprint v. APCC confirms assignees can sue when statutes are silent, yet here the statute is not silent—it draws a date-certain ownership line that courts must respect rather than invite a post-1996 market in assigned claims. Nothing in the colleagues’ discussion undermines that textual harmonization, so I adhere to affirmance for respondent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the present-tense phrasing in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—that whoever currently “owns the claim” may sue—and the general background rule (highlighted by Justice Sotomayor citing Sprint) that assignees can litigate. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 6082(a)(4) is a specific, date-certain ownership limitation for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, and reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post-cutoff acquisition would substantially nullify that calibrated restriction, contrary to RadLAX’s specific-over-general and anti-surplusage principles. Sprint helps only where Congress is silent; here Congress spoke in temporal terms, in a foreign-affairs-sensitive scheme where administrability and legitimacy counsel enforcing the line Congress drew rather than inviting an open-ended market in after-acquired claims. Nothing in the opposing textual argument genuinely undermines the harmonized reading that (a)(4) qualifies (a)(1)(A) for pre-1996 confiscations, so I would affirm.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best textual point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) speaks in the present tense—whoever “owns the claim” may sue—so later assignees look included. But, as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, that reading cannot be reconciled with § 6082(a)(4)’s explicit, date-certain ownership requirement for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations without reducing (a)(4) to near-surplusage; the specific-controls-the-general canon supplies the most coherent harmonization. Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Sprint v. APCC is helpful in framing the default rule on assignee standing, yet Sprint expressly operates in the absence of a contrary statutory restriction, and here Congress imposed one in temporal terms for this subset of claims. Under an original public meaning approach, the better reading is that (a)(4) qualifies (a)(1)(A) for pre-1996 confiscations, barring post-cutoff acquirers from suing on those older takings.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument is the plain present-tense phrase in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—any U.S. national who “owns the claim” may sue—which, in ordinary assignment practice, would include post-1996 assignees. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that reading functionally nullifies § 6082(a)(4)’s specific, date-certain ownership requirement for actions “based on” pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, creating surplusage and undermining Congress’s calibrated cutoff. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Sprint v. APCC strengthens my view that assignment is a default rule only when Congress has not spoken; here Congress did speak by tying eligibility for this category of older confiscations to ownership as of the cutoff date. Given the foreign-affairs sensitivity and the reliance interests implicated by expanding liability through a secondary market in claims, I do not see a sufficiently strong textual or precedential basis to override the limiting function of (a)(4).

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 6082(a)(1)(A) establishes a general cause of action for a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” but § 6082(a)(4) specifically limits actions “based on” property confiscated before March 12, 1996 to plaintiffs who owned the claim as of that date; reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post-1996 acquirers would largely nullify the explicit cutoff and violate the anti-surplusage principle. Under the general/specific canon, the more specific temporal limitation in (a)(4) controls the broader grant in (a)(1)(A), particularly in a statute touching foreign affairs where Congress often cabins liability carefully. That narrower reading also better serves institutional legitimacy by adhering to the text Congress wrote and avoiding an expansion of potentially diplomatically sensitive litigation beyond what the cutoff indicates. RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank supports harmonizing provisions by giving effect to the specific limitation rather than letting the general authorization swallow it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text controls: while § 6082(a)(1)(A) generally authorizes suit by a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” § 6082(a)(4) adds an express temporal limitation for actions “based on property confiscated before March 12, 1996,” requiring that the plaintiff have acquired ownership of the claim before that cutoff date. Reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to permit post‑1996 acquirers to sue would largely nullify § 6082(a)(4)’s date restriction, contrary to the ordinary rule that statutes should be read to give effect to every clause. Congress may define who may sue and when, and the courts must enforce those limits as written even if it narrows the remedial reach in particular cases. A strict textual reading therefore bars this suit because petitioner acquired the claim after March 12, 1996.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 6082(a)(4) operates as an express limitation on the otherwise general cause of action in § 6082(a)(1)(A): for actions “based on” property confiscated before March 12, 1996, Congress tied eligibility to ownership as of that cutoff date, and courts must give that limiting language operative effect rather than treat it as surplusage. Reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to allow any later-acquiring assignee to sue would largely nullify § 6082(a)(4) and expand liability beyond the class Congress specified, contrary to the general/specific canon and the ordinary rule that specific statutory restrictions control more general grants. That narrower construction also better accords with practical consequences and foreign-relations sensitivities embedded in Helms-Burton’s design, by preventing an open-ended market in post-1996 claim assignments from multiplying Title III exposure. Under a textualist approach, the Eleventh Circuit’s ownership-cutoff reading is the most faithful to the statute’s structure and expressed temporal limitation in § 6082(a)(4).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The statute’s limiting clause in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(4) is best read as an explicit ownership cutoff for pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, restricting Title III suits to plaintiffs who owned the claim as of that date; reading § 6082(a)(1)(A)’s broad “owns the claim” language to include post-1996 acquirers would largely nullify Congress’s temporal limitation. That straightforward textual constraint is especially important given the substantial reliance and foreign-relations consequences of expanding liability to an open-ended class of later assignees—an expansion Congress could have authorized more clearly. While assignees can have standing where a claim is validly assigned, Sprint Communications Co. v. APCC Services, Inc., 554 U.S. 269 (2008), supports that principle only absent a statutory restriction; here Congress appears to have imposed one. Respecting § 6082(a)(4)’s cutoff best aligns the cause of action with Congress’s calibrated remedial scheme rather than judicially broadening it.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 6082(a)(1)(A) creates a cause of action for a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” but Congress then added an express temporal limitation in § 6082(a)(4) for actions “based on” property confiscated before March 12, 1996—conditioning suit on the plaintiff having owned the claim as of that cutoff. Reading the statute as a whole, petitioner’s interpretation would largely drain § 6082(a)(4) of independent work, because anyone could acquire a pre-1996 claim after the fact and sue, effectively nullifying Congress’s date-certain restriction. That ownership-as-of requirement is a workability- and reliance-promoting line Congress was entitled to draw in a foreign-relations-sensitive statute, and the more coherent textual reading is that post-1996 assignees/successors are barred for pre-1996 confiscations. Given the clarity of the limiting clause, administrative or remedial-purpose arguments cannot override the enacted cutoff.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 6082(a)(1)(A) supplies the general cause of action for a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” but § 6082(a)(4) expressly limits “an action… based on a claim to property confiscated before March 12, 1996” to plaintiffs who acquired ownership of the claim before that date, making the cutoff a condition on who may sue for pre‑1996 confiscations. Reading the statute as a whole, the specific limitation in § 6082(a)(4) controls the general grant in § 6082(a)(1)(A), and petitioner’s interpretation would largely nullify Congress’s chosen temporal restriction by permitting post‑1996 assignees to proceed anyway. That text-based reading also respects separation-of-powers values by enforcing the liability boundary Congress enacted rather than expanding it by purposive inference. Where Congress has spoken in clear temporal terms (“before March 12, 1996”), our job is to apply that line as written, not to revise it in service of broader remedial aims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Title III ties the cause of action to a U.S. national who “owns the claim” and then adds an express limitation for pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations in § 6082(a)(4), which is most naturally read to require that the plaintiff have owned the claim as of the statutory cutoff date; otherwise that limiting clause does little independent work. Reading § 6082(a)(4) as a fixed-date ownership restriction respects Congress’s calibrated compromise in a foreign-affairs-sensitive statute and avoids expanding liability through post-enactment claim acquisitions—an approach consistent with judicial restraint and the Court’s practice of giving effect to statutory cutoffs as written. That interpretation is also more practically workable, because it provides a clear, administrable rule and protects reliance interests by preventing a potentially unlimited market in post-1996 claim assignments from broadening exposure beyond what Congress specified. In the absence of a clear statement authorizing post-cutoff acquirers to sue on pre-1996 confiscations, I would enforce the limitation Congress enacted in § 6082(a)(4).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The cause of action in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) is expressly qualified by § 6082(a)(4), which for property confiscated before March 12, 1996, limits actions to claims "owned by a United States national" as of that cutoff; reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post-1996 acquirers would largely nullify (a)(4)’s temporal-ownership restriction. A textualist reading harmonizes the provisions by treating (a)(4) as a specific limitation on the broader grant in (a)(1)(A), consistent with the canon that the specific controls the general. That approach also avoids surplusage by giving independent operative effect to Congress’s choice of a date-certain ownership cutoff, rather than reducing it to a mere reference point about confiscation timing. Under RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, the Court applies the specific-over-general principle to enforce targeted statutory limitations even when a neighboring provision is phrased more broadly.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III’s general cause of action in § 6082(a)(1)(A) for a U.S. national who “owns the claim” must be read together with the specific, date-based limitation in § 6082(a)(4), which addresses actions “based on property confiscated before March 12, 1996” and, on the most natural reading, cabins who may sue on those older confiscations to those who owned the claim as of the cutoff. Applying the specific-controls-the-general canon and the rule against surplusage, reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to permit post-1996 acquirers to sue for pre-1996 confiscations would substantially drain § 6082(a)(4) of independent work and expand liability beyond the narrower class Congress appears to have fixed. That construction also better aligns with procedural fairness and reliance interests by avoiding retroactive-like expansion of private enforcement to an enlarged pool of later assignees for long-ago confiscations, while leaving Congress free to broaden liability expressly if it chooses. Accordingly, I would affirm the Eleventh Circuit’s view that suits over pre-1996 confiscations are barred unless the plaintiff owned the claim as of March 12, 1996.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms–Burton Act allows a U.S. national to sue for “trafficking” in confiscated Cuban property when the plaintiff acquired ownership of the claim after the property was confiscated (and/or after the Act’s enactment), or whether the statute limits suits to claim-owners who held the claim at an earlier specified time.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms–Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (cause of action for any U.S. national who owns the claim to confiscated property against any person who traffics in such property), and related Title III definitional/limitations provisions governing who may sue and when (including provisions that tie eligibility to ownership timing and/or acquisition of the claim).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that the text and structure of Title III focus on the plaintiff’s present ownership of the claim—i.e., “any United States national who owns the claim”—and that Congress meant to create a broad remedial scheme to deter commercial exploitation of expropriated property and to provide compensation to victims (including successors-in-interest). On this view, the Eleventh Circuit adopted an atextual, extra-statutory timing restriction that narrows “owns the claim” and undermines Title III’s deterrent and compensation purposes; any statutory timing language should be read narrowly and in harmony with Title III’s express cause of action, not to bar successor owners categorically. The United States as amicus supports this reading, emphasizing foreign-policy interests in making Title III an effective mechanism against trafficking and in discouraging private actors from collaborating with the Cuban regime to profit from confiscated property.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents argue that Title III contains express eligibility limitations tied to when the plaintiff acquired the claim (and/or when the claim was held), and that Congress deliberately cabined the private right of action to avoid destabilizing foreign relations and to prevent a secondary market in Cuban-expropriation claims. They contend the Eleventh Circuit correctly harmonized the cause-of-action language with the Act’s limiting provisions so that only plaintiffs who held the claim by the statutory cutoff (rather than later acquirers) may sue. Respondents and their amici (travel and cruise industry groups) stress that petitioner’s interpretation would dramatically expand liability for ordinary travel-related commerce, create retroactive and unpredictable exposure, chill lawful travel and tourism-related activity, and generate international friction—outcomes Congress sought to mitigate through Title III’s carefully drawn limitations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the unqualified text in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize, we cannot read that general grant to silently displace Title III’s more specific timing/eligibility limits without rendering those provisions largely surplusage. Justice Sotomayor’s Landgraf/Hughes Aircraft concern strengthens the institutional case for a narrow construction: absent a clear statement, we should not interpret Title III to expand liability for past conduct via post-cutoff claim acquisitions. Under a whole-statute, minimalist approach, the best reading is that the cause of action is available only to plaintiffs who satisfy Congress’s express temporal gatekeeping, and petitioner does not.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is the breadth of § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but that clause cannot be read in isolation to override Title III’s specific temporal/eligibility limits without violating the whole-text and anti-surplusage canons. Justice Kavanaugh’s specificity-controls-generality framing is decisive for me as an originalist: the specific cutoff provisions define which claims are actionable and thereby qualify the general authorization to sue. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf concern further confirms that, absent a clear statement, we should not construe the statute to expand liability for past conduct via post-cutoff claim purchases. On the enacted text as a coherent scheme, Congress drew temporal lines that exclude petitioner as a later acquirer.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the breadth of § 6082(a)(1)(A) (“any United States national who owns the claim”), but read in context it cannot be allowed to swallow Congress’s specific timing/eligibility limits elsewhere in Title III without rendering those provisions effectively surplusage. Justice Kavanaugh’s specificity-controls-generality framing is persuasive under a whole-text approach: the statute’s targeted cutoff rules define which claims are actionable and thus who qualifies as an owner entitled to sue. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf concern reinforces the practical and textual problem with petitioner’s construction—post-cutoff purchases would dramatically expand liability for past conduct without a clear statement, inviting the very secondary market Congress plausibly meant to deter. Nothing raised in conference undermines my view that the better textual reading harmonizes the broad cause-of-action clause with the statute’s express gatekeeping restrictions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument remains the facially broad wording in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, reading that clause in isolation would substantially drain Congress’s specific timing/eligibility provisions of operative effect, contrary to the whole-statute and anti-surplusage canons. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf-based notice and retroactivity-adjacent concern also matters here: petitioner’s interpretation would permit later-acquired claims to trigger sweeping liability for past conduct without the clear statement we ordinarily require, especially in a foreign-affairs-calibrated scheme. I do not think “owns” can reasonably be treated as an unqualified present-tense trump card when Congress elsewhere drew deliberate cutoff lines that appear designed to prevent opportunistic claim trafficking and to cabin exposure. On pragmatic grounds, that harmonized reading better protects fairness and reliance interests while still honoring Congress’s chosen remedial compromise.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the breadth of § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but that phrase cannot be read as an unqualified present-ownership trigger without collapsing Title III’s explicit timing/eligibility limits elsewhere in the same scheme. Justice Kavanaugh’s anti-surplusage framing is the most persuasive articulation of that: if later-acquired claims may sue merely because they are now “owned,” Congress’s cutoff lines do little or no gatekeeping work. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf-based concern doesn’t drive my interpretation, but it reinforces the need for a clear statement before we construe the statute to expand liability for past trafficking through post-cutoff acquisitions. On my pragmatic textualist view, the best reading is the one that makes the provisions cohere and preserves the statute’s calibrated limits rather than treating them as optional.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the broad phrase in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but that language cannot be wrenched from Title III’s specific timing/eligibility provisions without violating the whole-text and anti-surplusage canons Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf framing matters even on my textualist terms: absent a clear statement, we should not read a general present-ownership clause to authorize a substantial expansion of liability for past conduct via post-cutoff claim acquisitions when Congress elsewhere drew explicit temporal lines. Treating this as a statutory cause-of-action boundary (as in Lexmark) best respects separation of powers by enforcing Congress’s enacted gatekeeping rather than enlarging the plaintiff class by implication. Nothing in the opposing textual argument overcomes the specificity-controls-generality principle, so petitioner—having acquired after the cutoff—falls outside the class Congress authorized to sue.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains the breadth of § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but that language cannot be read in isolation to override Title III’s specific temporal/eligibility limitations without making those limits largely surplusage under the whole-text canon. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf framing usefully underscores the institutional concern: petitioner’s reading would attach significant new legal consequences to past confiscations and pre-enactment conduct via post-cutoff claim purchases absent a clear statement, in a statute tightly calibrated for foreign-affairs consequences (including suspension authority). Justice Barrett’s specific-controls-general analysis reinforces that the general cause-of-action clause is best read as bounded by Congress’s explicit gatekeeping provisions rather than as a free-floating present-ownership trigger. Nothing raised in conference genuinely undermines that harmonizing interpretation, so I remain with respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest textual point remains the breadth of § 6082(a)(1)(A)—“any United States national who owns the claim”—but that phrase cannot be read atomistically when Title III elsewhere draws specific temporal/eligibility lines that define which claims are actionable and by whom. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf framing usefully underscores that petitioner’s reading would substantially expand liability for past conduct through post-cutoff acquisitions without the kind of clear statement we ordinarily require, especially in a foreign-affairs-sensitive statutory compromise. Justice Kavanaugh’s specificity-controls-generality and anti-surplusage analysis is decisive under a textualist whole-statute approach: the specific cutoff provisions must qualify the general cause-of-action language, or else Congress’s gatekeeping becomes largely ineffectual. Nothing presented undermines that harmonizing reading, so I would adhere to respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains the apparent breadth of the phrase “any United States national who owns the claim,” but reading that clause as an unqualified present-ownership trigger would, as Justice Kagan explains, make Congress’s timing/eligibility provisions do little or no gatekeeping work and invite claim-trafficking that undermines notice and procedural fairness. Chief Justice Roberts’s Landgraf framing further supports hesitation: absent a clear statement, we should not construe Title III to impose sweeping, hard-to-anticipate liability for past conduct based on post-cutoff assignments. Justice Gorsuch’s Lexmark point also fits my approach—this is a statutory cause-of-action question where Congress defined the plaintiff class, and courts should not expand it by isolating one broad phrase. None of these considerations is overcome by the textual breadth of “owns” standing alone, so I maintain my vote for Respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The cause-of-action clause—allowing suit by “any United States national who owns the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A)—must be read alongside Title III’s express eligibility limitations that tie actionable claims to specified ownership timing, reflecting Congress’s deliberate compromise to cabin liability and avoid creating a secondary market in claims. Under Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994), we presume Congress does not attach new legal consequences absent clear statement; reading § 6082(a)(1)(A) to permit post-cutoff purchasers to sue would substantially expand exposure for past confiscations and pre-enactment conduct without the clearest textual direction. A narrow construction that honors the statute’s timing restrictions best preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to the enacted limits rather than broad purposive expansion, and it respects Congress’s calibrated foreign-policy and federalism-related choices (including the Act’s suspension authority, 22 U.S.C. § 6085(c)). I would therefore affirm the limitation to claim-owners who held the claim by the statutory cutoff rather than later acquirers.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling question is what Congress actually enacted in Title III, and we must give effect to all of its text, not merely the broad opening clause “any United States national who owns the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A). Reading the cause-of-action provision together with Title III’s express eligibility limits tying suit to ownership at a specified time (the Act’s timing/ownership cutoff provisions governing who may sue), the better textual reading is that Congress restricted the private right of action to claimholders meeting that cutoff, thereby foreclosing later-acquired/trafficked-in claims and avoiding a congressionally disfavored secondary market in claims. That harmonized construction follows the ordinary rule that specific statutory limitations qualify a general grant and avoids converting a carefully cabined remedy into an open-ended assignment-based cause of action. Because petitioner acquired its claim after the relevant statutory cutoff, it falls outside the class Congress authorized to sue under Title III.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The cause-of-action clause in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (“any United States national who owns the claim”) must be read in harmony with Title III’s express eligibility and timing limitations governing who may sue and when; where Congress has imposed a cutoff tied to when the claim was held or acquired, courts are not free to treat that limiting language as surplusage. Consistent with the textualist approach reflected in Duncan v. Walker, 533 U.S. 167, 173 (2001), the statute’s inclusion of specific timing/eligibility language in certain provisions and not others signals deliberate line-drawing that this Court should enforce rather than override by appealing to broad remedial purpose. Petitioner's reading would effectively nullify the Act’s deliberate cabining and invite a secondary market in claims with sweeping, retroactive liability—practical consequences that confirm Congress likely meant the limitation to have real bite. As in Rotkiske v. Klemm, 589 U.S. 8 (2019), we should apply the statute as written, neither adding atextual exceptions nor stripping away clear constraints embedded elsewhere in the same statutory scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III’s general grant—allowing suit by “any United States national who owns the claim,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A)—must be read alongside Congress’s express eligibility limitations that tie who may sue to when the claim was held or acquired, which reflect a deliberate effort to cabin this private cause of action in a sensitive foreign-policy area. Allowing post-confiscation or post-enactment purchasers to sue would effectively expand civil liability beyond the class Congress specified and invite a secondary market in claims, creating the kind of unexpected, retroactive exposure that triggers the clear-statement rule. Under Landgraf v. USI Film Products, absent a clear indication Congress meant to authorize such expanded liability, courts should avoid interpretations that attach new legal consequences to past events through later-acquired claims; Hughes Aircraft reinforces that enlarging a statutory cause of action requires clarity, not implication. Given those constraints, the better reading is that Title III permits suits only by claim-owners who satisfied the statute’s timing-based eligibility requirements, preserving fairness and predictable notice for parties engaged in commerce tied to Cuba.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Although § 6082(a)(1)(A) begins broadly (“any United States national who owns the claim”), Title III must be read as a coherent whole, giving effect to Congress’s express eligibility and timing limitations elsewhere in the same section rather than treating the cause-of-action clause as unqualified. Under the harmonizing principle reflected in Ross v. Blake, courts may not create atextual exceptions, but they also must enforce statutory limits that Congress actually wrote; here, the structure and limiting provisions tying suit eligibility to when the claim was held are best read to bar later-acquired claims from triggering liability. That construction is also more workable and avoids turning Title III into an engine for claim trafficking—an outcome Congress plausibly sought to prevent given the Act’s calibrated private-enforcement scheme and foreign-relations sensitivities. On this reading, petitioner’s present-ownership focus cannot override the statute’s explicit temporal restrictions on who may sue and when.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title III’s cause-of-action clause—allowing suit by “any United States national who owns the claim to such property,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A)—must be read alongside Congress’s express eligibility limitations that tie actionable “claims” to ownership at specified times, rather than as an open-ended authorization for later-acquired claims. Under a textualist approach, courts do not treat statutory cause-of-action limits as mere purpose-frustrating technicalities; they define who may sue, and we enforce them as written rather than expanding them by reference to broad remedial aims. See Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118, 127–28 (2014) (the “zone-of-interests” and “cause-of-action” inquiries are questions of statutory interpretation, not freewheeling policy). Because Congress cabined this private right of action through timing/eligibility provisions, the better reading is that a plaintiff who acquired the claim only after the statutory cutoff falls outside the class Congress authorized to sue.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title III’s broad cause-of-action clause for “any United States national who owns the claim” in § 6082(a)(1)(A) must be read in harmony with Congress’s more specific eligibility/temporal limitations elsewhere in § 6082 and Title III’s definitional provisions; under the specificity-controls-generality principle, the specific timing restriction governs the general grant. Reading the statute to allow post-cutoff (or post-enactment) acquirers to sue would risk rendering the limiting language superfluous, contrary to the anti-surplusage canon and the Court’s ordinary practice of giving effect to all parts of an enacted scheme. Given the foreign-affairs sensitivities surrounding Cuba and Congress’s calibrated choice to open a private right of action only on defined terms, judicial restraint and practical workability counsel against expanding liability by interpretation beyond the statute’s express temporal boundaries. That narrower reading also avoids creating incentives for a secondary market in claims and unpredictable retroactive exposure—practical consequences Congress plausibly sought to mitigate through the Act’s eligibility limits.

Under Scalia & Garner’s harmonious-reading approach, we give effect to both the general cause-of-action language and the specific timing restrictions, and the specific limitation governs where it speaks directly to who may sue and when. Construing the statute to allow post-cutoff assignees to sue would largely nullify Congress’s deliberate temporal limitations and invite the very secondary market in expropriation claims Congress appears to have sought to avoid. This reading is consistent with the Court’s instruction to give effect to all statutory words “as far as possible,” Louisville & Nashville R. Co. v. Mottley, 219 U.S. 467, 475 (1911).

Under the whole-statute approach, we do not treat broad remedial phrasing as silently nullifying more specific limiting provisions, and we avoid interpretations that effectively read statutory cutoffs out of the Act. This reading accords with the interpretive principle that where Congress includes particular language in one section and different limitations elsewhere, courts must give independent effect to each provision rather than expand liability beyond the statute’s expressed temporal boundaries (Russello v. United States, 464 U.S. 16 (1983)).
